title: How does the JVM behave in containers/Kubernetes (UseContainerSupport, MaxRAMPercentage, request=limit, ExitOnOutOfMemoryError), and what went wrong before container awareness?
shortTitle: How the JVM behaves in containers and Kubernetes — UseContainerSupport, MaxRAMPercentage, request=limit, ExitOnOutOfMemoryError — and what went wrong before container awareness

s1_definition.profdef: Modern JVMs are container-aware: with `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` (on by default since Java 10 and backported to 8u191), the JVM reads the cgroup memory and CPU limits instead of the host's totals, so heap ergonomics and thread-pool sizing respect the container's allocation. You size the heap as a fraction of the limit with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, you set the Kubernetes memory request equal to the limit for predictable, non-overcommitted sizing, and you set `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` so an OutOfMemoryError terminates the JVM cleanly and the pod restarts. Before container awareness the JVM saw the whole host's memory and CPUs, so default heap and pool sizes were wildly too large, causing cgroup OOM-kills.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a bank clerk assigned one small room in a large building, but the clerk plans staffing as if the entire building were theirs — ordering furniture and hiring staff for the whole building. They instantly overflow their one room and get evicted. Container awareness is giving the clerk the correct room size so they plan for the room they actually have. Request equals limit is reserving that room exclusively so nobody else's overflow affects them, and ExitOnOutOfMemoryError is the clerk agreeing to leave immediately and be replaced if they ever run out of space, instead of staying and causing chaos.
s1_definition.oneliner: A container-aware JVM sizes itself from cgroup limits, not the host; set the heap as a percentage of the limit, make request equal limit, and exit on OOM so Kubernetes restarts the pod cleanly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Modern JVMs are container-aware: with `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` (on by default since Java 10 and backported to 8u191), the JVM reads the cgroup memory and CPU limits instead of the host's totals, so heap ergonomics and thread-pool sizing respect the container's allocation. You size the heap as a fraction of the limit with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, you set the Kubernetes memory request equal to the limit for predictable, non-overcommitted sizing, and you set `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` so an OutOfMemoryError terminates the JVM cleanly and the pod restarts. Before container awareness the JVM saw the whole host's memory and CPUs, so default heap and pool sizes were wildly too large, causing cgroup OOM-kills.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a bank clerk assigned one small room in a large building, but the clerk plans staffing as if the entire building were theirs — ordering furniture and hiring staff for the whole building. They instantly overflow their one room and get evicted. Container awareness is giving the clerk the correct room size so they plan for the room they actually have. Request equals limit is reserving that room exclusively so nobody else's overflow affects them, and ExitOnOutOfMemoryError is the clerk agreeing to leave immediately and be replaced if they ever run out of space, instead of staying and causing chaos.

**One line to remember:** A container-aware JVM sizes itself from cgroup limits, not the host; set the heap as a percentage of the limit, make request equal limit, and exit on OOM so Kubernetes restarts the pod cleanly.

sections.s2_technical:
Before container awareness, the JVM used operating-system calls that reported the physical host's resources. A pod limited to one gigabyte on a sixty-four-gigabyte node would see sixty-four gigabytes and, because the default maximum heap is one quarter of detected RAM, try to size the heap at sixteen gigabytes. The same happened with CPUs: the JVM saw all host cores and sized the common ForkJoinPool, GC threads, and other pools for the whole machine. The result was pods that either refused to start or, more insidiously, grew their heap until resident memory crossed the one-gigabyte cgroup limit and the kernel OOM-killed them, often under load and seemingly at random.

`-XX:+UseContainerSupport` fixed the memory side: the JVM now reads the cgroup memory limit and sizes default heap ergonomics from that. It also reads the CPU quota to size thread pools sensibly. This is on by default from Java 10 and was backported to late Java 8 updates, so any current JVM is container-aware unless you explicitly disable it.

`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` is how you control the heap in a container. Rather than a fixed `-Xmx` that breaks when the pod limit changes, you set the heap as a percentage of the detected limit, for example seventy-five percent for G1, leaving the rest for non-heap memory like Metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, and direct buffers. There are matching initial and minimum percentage flags. This keeps sizing correct automatically if the pod limit is later changed.

Request equals limit matters for predictability. In Kubernetes the request is what the scheduler reserves and the limit is the hard cgroup ceiling. If request is lower than limit, the pod can be scheduled onto a node that is overcommitted, and under memory pressure the node may reclaim or the pod may be throttled or killed unpredictably. Setting request equal to limit gives the pod a guaranteed quality-of-service class, so the memory it was sized for is genuinely reserved and the JVM's percentage-based heap is safe.

`-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` changes OOM behaviour from limping to failing fast. By default a heap OutOfMemoryError may be caught and the JVM may stagger on in a degraded state with threads dying and data structures half-built, which is worse than a clean death in a stateless service. With this flag the JVM terminates immediately on OOM; Kubernetes sees the container exit and restarts it, returning to a known-good state. You typically pair it with HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so you still capture evidence before exiting.

The senior nuance is to combine these: container support on (default), heap set by MaxRAMPercentage at a collector-appropriate value, Kubernetes request equal to limit for guaranteed QoS, exit on OOM for clean restarts, and a heap dump captured on the way out. You verify the JVM really sees the container limit by checking the effective heap at startup, not by trusting the manifest alone.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India lifted an old transfer service into Kubernetes on Java 8u151 without tuning. The JVM saw the whole node's memory and sized a huge default heap, so pods were OOM-killed within minutes. This is exactly the pre-container-awareness failure.

Problem 2 — After upgrading the JVM and enabling percentage-based sizing, the team still saw occasional unpredictable kills because request was less than limit and pods landed on overcommitted nodes. Setting request equal to limit and adding exit-on-OOM stabilized them. This is the request-equals-limit and clean-restart concern.

Our mini-project is a runnable container-awareness probe: it reports whether the JVM detected a container memory limit, the effective maximum heap, and the processors it sees, and it prints the recommended Kubernetes resource block and JVM flags. Classes are `ContainerAwarenessProbe` (driver), `ContainerEnvReporter` (reads available processors and heap max from the beans), and `K8sSizingAdvice` (produces the recommended manifest snippet and flags).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
container-awareness-probe/
├── pom.xml
├── Dockerfile
├── k8s/deployment.yaml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/kube/
            ├── ContainerAwarenessProbe.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── ContainerEnvReporter.java
```

Configuration (Kubernetes manifest with request == limit):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: transfer-service
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: transfer-service
          image: nbi/transfer-service:2.0.0
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "1Gi"    # request == limit → Guaranteed QoS
              cpu: "1"
            limits:
              memory: "1Gi"    # cgroup hard ceiling
              cpu: "1"
          env:
            - name: JAVA_OPTS
              value: >-
                -XX:+UseContainerSupport
                -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
                -XX:+UseG1GC
                -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
                -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
                -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/dumps
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Run with an explicit container memory limit; JVM should size heap from it
docker run --rm --memory=1g --cpus=1 nbi/transfer-service:2.0.0 \
  java -XX:+UseContainerSupport -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:+UseG1GC \
       -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
       -cp /app/container-awareness-probe-1.0.0.jar \
       com.bank.jvm.kube.ContainerAwarenessProbe

# Prove the difference: DISABLE container support and watch heap balloon
docker run --rm --memory=1g nbi/transfer-service:2.0.0 \
  java -XX:-UseContainerSupport -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
       -cp /app/container-awareness-probe-1.0.0.jar \
       com.bank.jvm.kube.ContainerAwarenessProbe
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the JVM starts inside a container limited to one gigabyte of memory and one CPU, with container support on and MaxRAMPercentage at seventy-five.

Step 1. At startup the JVM reads the cgroup memory limit, one gigabyte, because container support is enabled. It applies MaxRAMPercentage of seventy-five to that limit and sets the maximum heap to about seven hundred sixty-eight megabytes, leaving the rest for non-heap memory.

Step 2. `ContainerEnvReporter.reportHeapMax` reads the memory bean and logs that effective maximum. Because it reflects the container limit and not the host, the value is small and correct, and the heuristic check confirms it does not look like host sizing.

Step 3. `reportProcessors` reads available processors, which with container support reflects the CPU quota of one rather than all host cores. This matters because the JVM sizes the common ForkJoinPool, GC threads, and other pools from this number; an inflated value would create far too many threads.

Step 4. `K8sSizingAdvice.print` logs the recommended manifest guidance: request equals limit for guaranteed quality of service, MaxRAMPercentage of seventy-five, exit on OOM, and heap dump on OOM, with the computed heap figure for a one-gigabyte pod.

Step 5. If the same probe were run with container support disabled, the JVM would read the host's memory and compute a heap of many gigabytes, the heuristic would fire a severe warning, and in a real pod that would end in a cgroup OOM-kill. The comparison makes the failure mode concrete.

Step 6. The output gives the operator a definitive answer: the JVM is container-aware, the heap is sized from the limit, the CPU count is correct, and the recommended manifest and flags are printed — the exact checklist for safe deployment.

INFO: Effective max heap = 768MB (should reflect cgroup limit)

INFO: availableProcessors() = 1 (sizes thread pools / GC threads)

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  JVM start inside cgroup (limit = 1Gi, cpu = 1)
    │
    ├─ UseContainerSupport ON ──────────┐        ├─ UseContainerSupport OFF ─────┐
    │   reads cgroup limit = 1Gi         │        │   reads HOST memory = 64Gi     │
    │   MaxRAMPercentage 75% → ~768MB    │        │   default 1/4 host → ~16Gi     │
    │   availableProcessors = 1 (quota)  │        │   availableProcessors = 64     │
    ▼                                    ▼        ▼                                ▼
  heap + pools sized for the POD          heap + pools sized for the HOST
    │                                        │
    ▼                                        ▼
  RSS stays under 1Gi → healthy        RSS blows past 1Gi → cgroup OOMKill
    │
    ▼  (if a real OOM ever occurs)
  ExitOnOutOfMemoryError → clean exit → k8s restarts pod (+ heap dump captured)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Before the JVM was container-aware it sized itself from the physical host, not the container. A pod limited to one gigabyte on a large node would see all the host's memory and, because the default maximum heap is a quarter of detected RAM, try to size a sixteen-gigabyte heap, and it would likewise size thread pools and GC threads for all the host cores. The result was pods that either would not start or grew their resident memory until it crossed the cgroup limit and the kernel OOM-killed them, usually under load and apparently at random. That was the single most common surprise when teams first moved the JVM onto Kubernetes.

Container support fixed it. With UseContainerSupport, which is on by default since Java 10 and was backported to late Java 8 updates, the JVM reads the cgroup memory and CPU limits and sizes its ergonomics from those. On top of that I control the heap with MaxRAMPercentage rather than a fixed maximum, setting it to a collector-appropriate fraction like seventy-five percent so the heap tracks the pod limit automatically and leaves room for non-heap memory. I set the Kubernetes memory request equal to the limit so the pod gets a guaranteed quality-of-service class and the memory it was sized for is genuinely reserved, which removes the unpredictable kills that come from landing on an overcommitted node. And I set ExitOnOutOfMemoryError so a real OutOfMemoryError terminates the JVM immediately and Kubernetes restarts it to a known-good state instead of letting it limp, paired with HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so I still capture the evidence on the way out.

At National Bank of India we lifted an old transfer service onto Kubernetes on an early Java 8 build and the pods were OOM-killed within minutes because the JVM was sizing for the whole node; upgrading the JVM, switching to MaxRAMPercentage, making request equal to limit, and adding exit-on-OOM stabilized it completely. The habit I keep is to verify at startup that the effective heap actually reflects the cgroup limit rather than trusting the manifest alone, because the quickest way to catch a misconfiguration is to read what the JVM decided.
